1.support: We sought to determine the feasibility and impact of implementation of a protocol for use of esophageal balloon to set PEEP in obese patients in a community ICU.

2.support: All adult patients 18 years old or older requiring mechanical ventilation with class II and III obesity (BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2) with ARDS were eligible.

3.support: Twenty-nine mechanically ventilated adult patients with a median BMI of 45.8 kg/m2 with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

4.support: The report states 48 balloons were placed and 29 met inclusion criteria, but does not report how many eligible obese ARDS patients were not selected or whether all eligible patients received a balloon.

5.support: as a single-center study in a community setting, we were limited in sample size and may not be generalizable to all ICU settings.

6.support: The esophageal catheter used was the CooperSurgical 5F catheter, 47-9005... PEEP was titrated based on PL at end expiration (End Exp PL) until it approached 0 (±2) cm H2O

7.support: Outcomes measured include PEEP, oxygenation, and driving pressure (DP) before and after esophageal manometry at 4 and 24 hr.

8.support: Data were extracted directly from the electronic medical records by investigators.

9.support: Comparison of ventilator settings between baseline, 4 hours, and 24 hours are shown in Table 2.

10.support: A Wilcoxon signed rank test was used to assess the difference in the PEEP, S/F ratios, Fio2, and driving pressure (DP) pre- and postesophageal balloon placements at 4 and 24 hours.

11.support: Ventilator settings, ventilator pressures, and hemodynamic vasopressor support were obtained before esophageal balloon placement and after optimization at 4 and 24 hours.

12.support: The intervention (esophageal-manometry-guided PEEP titration) was applied at the individual patient level, not at a group level.

nih.rationale: Rating Fair: the study question was clear (item 1), eligibility criteria were prespecified (item 2), patients were representative of the target obese ARDS population (item 3), the intervention was protocolized and consistently delivered (item 6), outcomes were objective physiological measures (item 7), complete 24-hour follow-up was achieved (item 9), and formal pre-to-post statistical testing with p values was performed (item 10). It is not Good because there was no power/sample size justification for the small n=29 cohort (item 5), no blinding of outcome assessors in this retrospective chart review (item 8), only a single pre-intervention measurement rather than an interrupted time-series design (item 11), and enrollment of all eligible patients could not be determined (item 4).
